tip: fy (my) nasal-mutates the next word, turning g into ng: gwaith becomes ngwaith in fy ngwaith.
o (of) soft-mutates the noun after it: cadeiriau becomes gadeiriau, so digon o gadeiriau means enough chairs.
a (and) aspirate-mutates a following p, t or c: pob becomes phob here in a phob bendith.
i'w is i plus ei (to its) and it soft-mutates the verb: gwastraffu becomes wastraffu in i'w wastraffu, to waste it.
The -wch ending marks a plural or polite command: Arhoswch means wait, said to more than one person or formally.
Welsh has no all-purpose word for no; you echo the verb. Nac ydy answers an ydy question in the negative.
their brackets the noun as eu ... nhw: eu gardd nhw means their garden, with nhw reinforcing eu.
trafferth is feminine, so it soft-mutates after the article y: y drafferth means the trouble.
Wedi'r cyfan is a set phrase meaning after all, used to open a concluding thought.
eisiau (want) skips the usual yn: you say ddim eisiau, never ddim yn eisiau.
The negative past of cael starts with Ch: Ces becomes Ches, so Ches i ddim means I didn't get.
as ... as is mor ... ag: mor syml ag means as simple as.
ei (her) leaves gardd unchanged and pairs with hi; ei (his) would soft-mutate it to ardd. So ei gardd hi is her garden.
Welsh shows having something with gyda: gyda ni literally with us is how you say we have.
fy nasal-mutates c into ngh: cefnder becomes nghefnder in fy nghefnder, my cousin.
Comparatives add -ach and take na or nag: bwysicach nag iechyd means more important than health.
ei (her) adds an h before a vowel: amynedd becomes hamynedd in ei hamynedd, her patience.
Fronting a phrase then adding sy'n gives emphasis: Fy modryb sy'n gwneud means it is my aunt who makes.
Pe opens an unreal past condition: Pe baen ni wedi gadael means if we had left.
ei (her) aspirate-mutates a following t into th: traed becomes thraed in ei thraed, her toes.
dwy (feminine two) soft-mutates the noun after it: gwlad becomes wlad in i'r ddwy wlad, the two countries.
